stages.name: Pre-engagement
stages.definition: Prospective newcomers find a project of interest, contact its community, and sometimes make early contributions.

stages.name: Proposal preparation
stages.definition: Applicants turn their interest into a feasible project plan through proposal preparation.

stages.name: Applicant review and selection
stages.definition: Mentors use proposals to assess applicants’ readiness and project fit, and select contributors within the organization’s mentoring capacity.

stages.name: Bonding and initial onboarding
stages.definition: Selected contributors learn project tools, workflows, and community norms as working relationships begin to form.

stages.name: Contributing and mentoring
stages.definition: Contributors move into substantive project work, building skills through mentors’ guidance and feedback.

stages.name: Contribution review
stages.definition: Review and revision inform decisions about acceptance or integration. Issue, pull-request, and commit interactions support an ongoing cycle between contributing and review.

stages.name: Evaluation and completion
stages.definition: Milestones and midterm and final pass/fail decisions assess contributors’ progress and participation alongside the ongoing contribution-review cycle.

stages.name: Retention and role transition
stages.definition: After graduation, contributors may continue participating in their communities, sometimes returning as mentors. This transition can renew the mentoring cycle.

stages.name: Governance
stages.definition: Rules, accountability, coordination, and mentor capacity support activities across the pipeline. Governance is a cross-stage layer in the RQ1 figure, rather than an additional chronological stage.

excerpts.text: there is a very huge wave that comes [3 or 4 months] before GSOC... like a single contributor is making 5 PRs... so it gets very overwhelming for reviewers.
They just AI it up, complete it, and say yeah, I understood everything. Even though they probably didn't.
A lot of AI-generated proposals [contained] 'here is the proposal you asked for'... They didn't even bother to check.
[The organization] accepted a contributor... [then] found out that this person does not know how to use Git... [or] run shell commands. But their proposal looked correct...
AI is meaning that those tasks [of different difficulty levels] are less of a differentiator and we need to meet these people in person more often, which takes more time
Easy access to AI has made it easier for applicants to abuse the application process

Before [AI], people would ask many more questions while progressing to a solution... review went much better because you had an understanding of what the person was thinking. Now you have to be more guarded.
It has become very easy for [newcomers] to raise PRs and fix the bugs... But we asked them, why did you make this change? They gave us an AI-generated response.
[A mentee] told me that I won't be able to create more PRs until my AI limit renews.

Earlier, [a contributor] would come to me with a problem, and I didn't know the solution either, so we both would deep dive... There was serious mental effort... [that] helped me grow along with my contributor.
I had to pay more attention to reminding people what the program rules were, aside from what our project-specific guidelines are.
If it's easier to write a submission, then it's harder to review a submission... even the mentors are humans. They can't review everything.
The only significant change has been the amount of effort we're putting into reviewing PRs.
The code PRs are so long that it's 5,000 lines of code. And they expect us to review the complete PR within 2 days.
If [an] AI disclosure [is made]... we run an extra set of tests... [review takes] maybe 20, 30% more.
I can no longer trust that a human has actually checked what they are doing
We're having lots of incremental and small bits and modules [that were] very costly to maintain
When we give AI a prompt and it gets something working and we just push it, it can be disastrous... you never know what AI missed; it could be a security threat.
The AI review pointed out syntax-related issues [such as] unused functions or cleanups... but not necessarily in terms of the business logic or the mathematical [logic] because they can get complex.
Every other week I see a thread about whether I should fail this contributor because they did not follow my LLM guidelines
I am worried [about] how much [contributors] are learning and [whether they will] stick to the project and the community
Folks drop off because they get automated replies or generic responses
LLMs are trained on data that is not attributable... we might be violating license agreements with other open source projects.

Some [projects] have an explicit policy saying we do not accept AI contributions. Most have an AI disclosure policy... [others say] it's okay if you use AI as long as... the quality is high enough that it doesn't look AI-generated.
People are moving to self-hosted [forges] because they may not want AI trained on their code
It's a drain on their time... [Organizations] want new people to join and grow, not... prompt a tool [and transfer review work].
[AI disclosure] causes extra work for mentors... we have to stay up to date [on] whether they're following the rules and look for cues [but] that's necessary.
I've been a lot more worried on the impact it has on mentors. It does create fatigue... implication in terms of workload.

The overall amount of effort had gone up exponentially to something we can't keep up with... We have not participated in GSoC 2026. I don't think we will be participating again... It is just not in our bandwidth.
The contributor was facing issues while setting up the project... AI was a huge help for me as a mentor because I was able to quickly debug and answer their questions
If I had mentored three or four years ago, I would have struggled to manage the time

GitHub Copilot first reviews [a pull request]... and they add some comments... common [issues] are detected automatically, and the contributor can immediately get feedback... without waiting for a human.

impacts.name: Talent recruitment and entry
impacts.definition: GSoC helps OSS organizations identify and recruit motivated, capable newcomers.

excerpts.text: We got most of the contributors from [GSoC]... this has been one of those hot spots [for newcomers].

implications.text: GenAI makes it harder to identify capable, committed newcomers.
GenAI makes screening take more effort.

impacts.name: Developing trustworthy community members
impacts.definition: GSoC develops contributors trusted with responsibility through demonstrated understanding and commitment.

excerpts.text: We are judging the students even before they apply... [based on] six months contributi[on] for us... even if [they] does an AI-generated application, we know [they are] capable.

implications.text: GenAI weakens artifacts as evidence of competence.
GenAI demands greater mentor attention to building trust.
GenAI increases the importance of developing trusted contributors.

impacts.name: Skills development and career signal
impacts.definition: GSoC develops technical skills, judgment, and professional competence and signals career readiness.

excerpts.text: GSoC has been pretty monumental... helped me secure Linux Foundation opportunities, grants... and the technical competence to see them through.

implications.text: GenAI dependence may weaken skills, judgment, and career credibility.

impacts.name: Maintainability of funded contributions
impacts.definition: GSoC funds verified, maintainable improvements to under-resourced OSS projects.

excerpts.text: GSoC has attracted many contributors we would not normally have gotten... helped us solve longstanding issues nobody was in the mood of working on.

implications.text: Unreliable GenAI output and maintenance debt threaten lasting value of GSoC-funded work.

impacts.name: Institutionalization of governance practices
impacts.definition: GSoC establishes lasting organizational routines for OSS mentoring and governance.

excerpts.text: All the decisions we make, we write it down... we won't repeat the same thing again and again every year

implications.text: OSS policy fragmentation and GenAI-driven enforcement demands may strain governance.
GenAI assistance can improve organizational routines.

impacts.name: Community growth, diversity and vitality
impacts.definition: GSoC builds a diverse, lasting contributor community through sustained newcomer engagement.

excerpts.text: GSoC gives people who are new to open source a chance to contribute and hopefully keep contributing... the aim is mostly keeping the organization alive and thriving.

implications.text: GenAI-driven distrust and additional workload may hinder welcoming, diverse and engaged OSS participation.

impacts.name: Contributor-to-steward renewal
impacts.definition: GSoC renews OSS communities by developing contributors into committed maintainers and future mentors.

excerpts.text: Almost 70% of [2026 mentors] had been our previous students... we are growing mentors who can guide the next generation of contributors.

implications.text: GenAI-weakened project attachment may disrupt the renewal pathway.
GenAI-driven mentor withdrawal threatens support for future capacity.

impacts.name: Mentor motivation and retention
impacts.definition: GSoC sustains mentor participation through personal and community benefits and manageable workloads.

excerpts.text: GSoC has had a huge impact on my career... [and] gave me a chance to mentor... I've always been on the receiving end of [GSoC]... helping someone else was a great experience for me.

implications.text: GenAI-driven verification burdens and reduced satisfaction may weaken continued participation.
GenAI assistance reduces effort required for certain mentoring tasks.

strategyGroups.name: Establishing trust in applicants
strategyGroups.description: Build evidence of readiness beyond polished proposals and entry contributions.

strategyGroups.name: Governing GenAI use and maintaining accountability
strategyGroups.description: Choose a GenAI boundary while keeping understanding, checking, and responsibility with people.

strategyGroups.name: Sharing guidance and verification across the program
strategyGroups.description: Share support across organizations while retaining local autonomy.

strategies.name: Selecting applicants by prior contribution trajectory
strategies.definition: Judge applicants by months of visible work before they apply (e.g., merged PRs, follow-through on issues, and responses to review feedback) beyond proposal quality.

excerpts.text: We are judging the students even before they apply... [based on] six months contributi[on] for us... even if [they] does an AI-generated application, we know [they are] capable.

One thing we looked out for this year was a consistent history of high quality contributions prior to GSoC... all of [the selected candidates] had very good PRs already merged... interactions genuine enough to make us trust... they were reviewing their own code.

strategies.name: Live interviews to verify applicants' unaided ability
strategies.definition: Test applicants in real time through screen-share, live coding, scenario questions, or verbal explanation to confirm that they, not GenAI, can do the work.

excerpts.text: We do not go by the applications. We try to take face-to-face interviews, video interviews with screen sharing on... scenario-based questions... [and] make them write the code in front of us in the editor
Next years... we will try to conduct interviews before selecting... are they really strong enough without AI?

strategies.name: Entry tasks that require project-specific understanding
strategies.definition: Redesign, stagger, or curate starter tasks so they depend on the project's own processes and cannot be solved by a bare prompt.

excerpts.text: [We need tasks requiring] more cognitive thought and understanding of our processes... so that just a prompt with the task will not be able to produce the output

strategies.name: Rewarding honest, rule-following GenAI use in selection
strategies.definition: Lower the priority of applicants with undisclosed or rule-breaking GenAI use while offering revision opportunities to borderline cases.

excerpts.text: [Mentors] did try not to select folks who were using AI, not because of a refusal to accept any AI code, but... to compensate for the abundance of applicants... using AI without paying attention to rules.
Candidates... looked eligible... but wherever we had some hint [that] they might be using LLMs and were not honest... we put them on a lower priority list.
Some of [AI-generated proposals] came back and rewrote it. And I was like, okay, this is fine.
We took the effort of manually going through each proposal [in a filtering session]... marked AI slop proposals as not fit... stack-ranked all the non-slop proposals [and] gave a chance to improve.

strategies.name: Banning GenAI for specific outputs with explicit exceptions
strategies.definition: Restrict or ban GenAI assistance in specified outputs (e.g., proposals) or activities (e.g., onboarding) while explicitly allowing bounded uses (e.g., language help).

excerpts.text: I used AI for documenting the project... AI is good for documentation... I trust AI on this.
We specifically asked in our project description: please do not submit any code using AI.
I have a strict ban on artificial intelligence use
You may not use AI or LLMs in any way

strategies.name: Allowing GenAI conditionally: “assistant, not owner”
strategies.definition: Permit GenAI assistance within local rules when contributors understand, check, and take ownership of the output.

excerpts.text: We do follow a practice that always recommend to use AI as long as you know what you are working on and how it is working
[AI] is a tool... [mentees may] check grammar, bugs, and style... We allow [that], and that's fine
You are using AI as your assistant. AI is not your owner
You control the AI; you don't let the AI control you

strategies.name: Judging quality, not authorship
strategies.definition: Judge whether contributions work and meet quality expectations instead of treating who wrote them as decisive.

excerpts.text: Whether it has been generated by AI, whether it has been human-written... if things are working fine, then people are happy with it.
Code quality is more important than flagging someone for using AI.

strategies.name: Using GenAI for mentoring support
strategies.definition: Use GenAI to assist routine mentoring tasks, such as onboarding, submission triage, summaries, progress tracking, or first-pass review.

excerpts.text: We do have GitHub Copilot [and] use that on occasion to review larger changes... It is much better than us at catching things [like] security, subtle bugs, edge cases.
One was I quickly got AI to review the whole PR code base... the second thing, I myself reviewed the PR

strategies.name: Teaching contributors to use GenAI responsibly
strategies.definition: Teach contributors, through explicit instruction or by modeling practice, to read, test, and take responsibility for GenAI-assisted work while retaining human decisions.

excerpts.text: We gave [contributors] written instructions on what we are expecting with the use of AI, and we encourage them to use it... [but] they shouldn't be completely dependent upon it.
You can use my expertise to help you to understand how to check things, but I am not being your checker... My role is to mentor you to develop your skills.
If it breaks, you need to know how to identify and fix the issue

strategies.name: Keeping final decisions with human reviewers
strategies.definition: Keep responsibility for reviewing and accepting submitted contributions with mentors instead of delegating verification to GenAI.

excerpts.text: Even after AI said it was good to go, then we have to manually review it.

strategies.name: Treating GenAI-suspicion cues as prompts for closer review
strategies.definition: Use suspicious patterns of generated code or provenance checks to decide what to examine more closely, not to reject automatically, as attribution remains unclear.

excerpts.text: It is next to impossible to confidently attribute something [as] AI-generated... we need to look for... heuristics. We can't really depend on hard and fast rules. But when we do find definitive proof... we swiftly ban users from our repos.

strategies.name: Asking contributors to explain their code in review
strategies.definition: Ask contributors to explain their decisions and demonstrate their work; inability to explain is what disqualifies a contribution.

excerpts.text: I'll ask little things like, ‘Why did you choose to do it this way?' If they can't answer, then... [it is] a sign [of AI use]. But I don't accuse them immediately... It's through a discussion, ‘How did you check it?', that you can have a learning relationship.
If [the contributor uses] AI properly, understands the logic, and makes you understand it, it will be almost impossible to tell whether AI [was] used.

We sometimes ask them to clarify their prompt. If they use AI right, we probably won't see it; if they use it to do their job instead of themselves for them, we will. We don't have a philosophical rejection of AI.

strategies.name: Requiring contributors to disclose GenAI use
strategies.definition: Ask contributors to disclose whether and how they used GenAI so mentors can adjust review checks targetedly.

excerpts.text: It would be better if [the organization] put [AI disclosure] as a strict guideline so mentors don't have to do... guessing work... mentees [should] explicitly list whether and how they use LLMs.

strategies.name: Coordinating GenAI guidance across the program
strategies.definition: Share guidance, resources, disclosure mechanisms, and lessons learned across participating organizations, while each organization retains autonomy over its own GenAI rules.

excerpts.text: [GSoC could] come up with a guideline [for AI usage]... but each and every organization is differently structured. They follow their own rules along with the GSoC rules... generalized practices could be spread along.
At the program level... require a strict form where the mentee discloses in what capacity they're using AI... [so that] eases the burden from each community individually enforcing those rules

[At the program level,] having an AI... scan proposals... and flag it if they think it's... LLM-generated. Not to say that we would immediately disregard that person, but just as an external flag so that we don't have to... unpick everything... we suspect this might be LLM-generated, and then you can look through with that lens.

boundary: Prohibit GenAI in specified outputs and stages.
List permitted exceptions, such as accessibility or translation.
Accept unpolished work rather than allowing unlisted GenAI polishing.
entry: Require work covered by the ban to be done without GenAI.
Ask applicants to demonstrate their skills directly if their readiness is unclear.
Apply published consequences for policy violations and allow revisions where permitted.
mentoring: Teach contributors to break down problems, use project documentation, and develop their own solutions for work covered by the ban.
Ask contributors to walk through their implementation and how they tested it, and use gaps in understanding to guide further mentoring.
Have contributors make requested revisions themselves with GenAI allowed only for listed exceptions.
governance: Review disputed cases to separate confirmed violations from uncertain attribution.
Check whether the rules or the process for fixing or disputing a violation were unclear, and whether enforcement took time away from mentoring support.
Update the examples, exceptions, and evidence expectations upon review.

boundary: Restrict GenAI by default, allowing only a short list of low-risk uses (e.g., code explanations).
Require contributors to develop the substance of their work.
Require approval and output checks for other uses.
entry: Ask applicants to disclose any permitted GenAI use and how they checked its output.
Probe their own reasoning with follow-up questions, and confirm that any use beyond the list was approved.
Look closely at questionable submissions through discussion before deciding.
mentoring: Teach contributors to develop core solutions themselves with GenAI use only for permitted low-risk assistance.
Show contributors how to check GenAI suggestions against documentation, code behavior, or tests before relying on it.
Ask contributors to explain how bounded GenAI use shaped their reasoning, and target extra review or tests at the affected parts.
governance: For each permitted use, check whether contributors follow the rules and can stand behind the output.
Keep, narrow, or expand the permitted list, expanding only when the results are consistently good.
Document how additions are approved and checked, and keep only the disclosure that helps review.

boundary: Permit GenAI for supporting tasks (e.g., documentation or testing) rather than core work.
List exclusions for each output or stage.
Require contributors to review, adapt, and check output and to keep their reasoning and decisions.
entry: Allow GenAI for supporting tasks in the application, but not for core proposal or entry tasks.
Ask applicants to explain their independently developed their ideas or task solutions.
Ask applicants to explain how they reviewed, adapted, and checked generated outputs.
mentoring: Teach contributors to develop the core work themselves and use GenAI for supporting tasks.
Ask contributors to inspect GenAI output for wrong assumptions, missing cases, and inconsistencies before mentor review.
Ask contributors to explain core decisions and check that supporting material alongside the major changes reflects what the code does.
governance: Check supporting tasks for recurring inaccuracies or mismatches with the core implementation.
Identify where GenAI help crossed into core work, obscured decisions, or shifted corrections onto mentors.
Update the exclusions for each output or stage, and the checking instructions for supporting tasks.

boundary: Permit GenAI across development, including implementation; state only necessary project limits.
Require contributors to understand and check outputs.
Require contributors to make decisions and answer review questions themselves.
entry: Accept GenAI-assisted work and assess whether it works and meets project requirements.
Ask applicants to explain their choices, demonstrate their checks, and respond to feedback themselves.
mentoring: Teach contributors to define problems, break down tasks, give GenAI useful context, and evaluate assisted or generated solutions.
Guide contributors to adapt generated code, test it within the project, and resolve failures before submission.
Review contributions against project requirements, and have contributors diagnose and fix work that fails, regardless of how it was produced.
governance: Review GenAI-assisted work for whether contributors could explain, fix, and maintain it.
Note where mentors had to reconstruct the reasoning or fix the work themselves.
Revise the project limits, contributor responsibilities, and mentoring guidance where gaps appeared.

boundary: Integrate GenAI into daily development within security, privacy, and licensing rules.
Expect contributors to use GenAI as a working tool.
Hold contributors responsible for diagnosing and fixing failures in what they submit.
entry: Ask applicants to demonstrate how they use GenAI on a project-specific task, including how they provide context and evaluate suggestions.
Ask them to demonstrate how they would diagnose and correct failures in the generated output.
mentoring: Model how to give GenAI project context, inspect its outputs, and decide which to use, change, or reject.
Bring GenAI-assisted attempts into routine mentor discussions, with contributors presenting their checks, decisions, and open questions.
Use planned checkpoints to confirm that contributors still understand their work and can diagnose and fix failures as GenAI use grows.
governance: Review where routine GenAI use supported learning and where contributors struggled to catch or fix faulty output.
Update approved tools and their access limits, mentoring routines, and checkpoints to close those gaps.
Widen project scope or automation only if mentor can still verify the work and contributors keep learning.

capacity.name: GenAI boundary
actions: Check that mentors have enough time and expertise to apply the chosen stance.
Assign mentors to learning support and final review, and Org Admins to policy and workload coordination.
Pause new GenAI permissions when capacity is limited.

capacity.name: Entry and early preparation
actions: Match contributor numbers and project scope to available mentoring capacity.
Publish entry requirements, check them before detailed review, and stagger starter tasks when volume is high.
Use additional screening when applicants' readiness is hard to trace.

capacity.name: Mentoring, review, and evaluation
actions: Budget mentor time for the work your stance adds.
Reuse reviewed guides and automated checks for routine work; use GenAI support only where the stance permits.
Have contributors check their work and prepare explanations before review.

capacity.name: Governance
actions: Check review backlogs, missed mentoring discussions, and mentor feedback at agreed intervals.
Cap open submissions per contributor or narrow tasks when review falls behind.
If overload persists, adjust estimated contributor numbers next cycle.
